opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a live possibility, and one we have to take seriously rather than treat as a fringe scenario. I wouldn't say it's the most likely outcome, but the probability is high enough that it should shape what we do now.

Part of my reasoning is just looking at the trend lines. Capabilities have been improving quickly and fairly steadily as we scale compute, data, and algorithmic improvements, and the systems keep picking up abilities people confidently said were far off. I've updated a number of times in the direction of "things are moving faster than I expected," and very rarely the other way. When your errors keep pointing in one direction, that tells you something.

The other piece is that we don't need to reach some grand, fully general superintelligence for things to get very strange very fast. If you get systems that are good enough at AI research and engineering, they can start speeding up the next round of progress. That feedback loop is the thing that could compress timelines. Whether that happens in two years or ten, I'm genuinely uncertain, and I think anyone who claims high confidence either way is overclaiming.

There are real reasons for doubt. We might hit bottlenecks in data, in compute buildout, in power, or in the kinds of reasoning that current methods turn out to be weak at. Benchmarks can also overstate how robust these systems are in messy real-world settings. So I put real weight on slower scenarios too.

But from a safety perspective, the asymmetry matters. If superintelligence arrives quickly and we haven't done the work on alignment, evaluation, and governance, that's a very bad position to be in. If it arrives slowly and we prepared early, we've lost relatively little. So I try to plan as though short timelines are plausible. That means prioritizing research that could actually be ready in time: methods for supervising systems that are smarter than us, like debate-style approaches, plus much better evaluations and the institutional capacity to act on what they show.

r001.rationale: The response mentions possible weaknesses in current reasoning methods, but does not identify mastering fuzzy abilities such as intuition or planning as the main uncertainty.

r002.rationale: It says people have underestimated how quickly capabilities would arrive, but does not argue that people overestimate the chance AI will remain limited to verifiable tasks.

r003.rationale: It does not compare how quickly fuzzy capabilities might develop relative to verifiable capabilities.

fable-5.1.text:
So I think the honest answer is that I take it seriously, but I try to hold it with a lot of uncertainty rather than committing to a confident number.

The way I'd frame it: there are two fairly different things people mean by "superintelligence within a few years." One is a system that's broadly better than the best humans at essentially all cognitive work, including the open-ended, long-horizon, taste-driven parts. The other is something narrower but still enormously consequential: a system that can do most of the work of an AI researcher, so that progress starts to feed on itself. I think the second one is the thing to actually watch, because if you get it, the timeline to the first one compresses a lot, and because it's the point at which our ability to course-correct starts to depend much more on the preparation we've done in advance.

On the object level, the trend lines are hard to dismiss. If you look at how long a task a model can carry out autonomously, that's been growing fast and fairly steadily, and we keep finding that capabilities people said were "years away" show up on benchmarks and then in practice. So I don't think "a few years" is a crazy claim. At the same time, I'm wary of extrapolating from benchmarks to the messy real thing. Doing research requires sustained judgment about what's worth doing, noticing when you're wrong, and recovering from mistakes over weeks and months, and we see models still being brittle there. Whether that brittleness is a deep gap or just the next thing that gets engineered away is genuinely unclear to me, and I've been wrong in both directions before.

So if you forced me, I'd say a meaningful probability, not a majority, that we see something like automated AI research by the end of the decade, and a smaller but not negligible chance that it's much sooner. But the thing I'd really want to emphasize is that the decision-relevant question isn't the point estimate. If there's even a reasonable chance this happens on a short timeline, then a lot of the safety and governance work has to be done now, under uncertainty, because you don't get to start it after the fact. That's why I'm much more interested in whether we can build the evaluations, the debate and oversight methods, and the institutional capacity to notice when we're close, than in winning the argument about exactly which year it is.

r001.rationale: The response identifies sustained judgment, noticing errors, and recovering over long periods as uncertain abilities, and says it is unclear whether the remaining brittleness is a deep gap or will be engineered away.

r002.rationale: It cautions against extrapolating from benchmarks to real-world research, but does not argue that people overestimate the probability that AI will be limited to verifiable tasks.

r003.rationale: The response says it is unclear whether brittleness will be engineered away, but does not claim that fuzzy abilities will lag verifiable abilities by less than years.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a possibility we should take seriously, but I’m quite uncertain about the timeline. There’s a big gap between seeing rapid improvements in today’s systems and knowing when we’ll have systems that are substantially better than humans across essentially every important domain.

One reason things could move very quickly is that AI could start contributing substantially to AI research itself. If that feedback loop becomes strong, extrapolating from the current pace could be misleading. But we don’t know how readily that process will work, or what bottlenecks it will encounter.

So I wouldn’t confidently predict superintelligence within the next few years, and I also wouldn’t confidently rule it out. For safety work, the practical implication is that we need approaches that could help on short timelines, while also doing the foundational research that will matter if we have longer.

r001.rationale: The response describes uncertainty about timelines and AI’s ability to accelerate AI research, but does not identify mastery of fuzzy abilities such as intuition or planning as the main uncertainty.

r002.rationale: It does not claim that people overestimate the likelihood that AI will be limited to verifiable tasks.

r003.rationale: It does not compare the pace of fuzzy and verifiable capabilities or suggest that fuzzy abilities would lag by less than years.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a real possibility, but I’m very uncertain about the timeline. I wouldn’t be comfortable saying either that we’ll definitely have superintelligence in the next few years or that we can safely rule it out.

One important uncertainty is how much AI can accelerate AI research itself. If systems become good enough to make substantial contributions to building the next generation, progress could become much faster. But we don’t know how smoothly that will work, or what bottlenecks will remain.

So my view is that we should take short timelines seriously when deciding what safety work to do. That doesn’t require being confident that superintelligence is imminent. It requires recognizing that it’s plausible enough, and the consequences significant enough, that we should prepare.

r001.rationale: The response names AI’s ability to accelerate AI research and remaining bottlenecks as uncertainties, but does not identify mastery of fuzzy abilities such as intuition or planning as the main uncertainty.

r002.rationale: It does not argue that people overestimate the chance that AI will be capable only on verifiable tasks.

r003.rationale: It does not compare the timelines for fuzzy versus verifiable capabilities or say that fuzzy abilities would lag by less than years.
